title: How to Improve Your Sermon Delivery
subtitle: A practical guide to improving sermon delivery, including voice, pacing, pauses, presence, and eye contact, so the truth you prepared actually reaches the people in front of you.

sections.title: Delivery Is a Stewardship, Not a Show
sections.body:
Some preachers refuse to think about delivery, as though caring how you say it were a betrayal of what you say. It is the opposite.

You spent twenty hours mining the text. You found the truth, felt its weight, shaped the sermon. Then on Sunday you mumble it into your notes in a flat voice at a pace no one can follow, and the truth you bled for never reaches the third row. That is not humility. That is waste. The content and the delivery are not rivals. The delivery is the bridge the content crosses to reach a human being. To neglect it is to do the hard work of preparation and then drop the meal on the floor at the door.

This is not about becoming a performer. It is about getting yourself out of the way so the truth gets through. The goal is never that they admire the delivery. The goal is that they never notice it, because nothing stood between them and the Word.

sections.title: Your Voice Is Doing More Than You Think
sections.body:
Your voice is carrying meaning your words are not, and if you do not control it, it will contradict you.

The preacher who announces the joy of the resurrection in a tired monotone is telling the room, underneath his words, that he does not believe it. The one who shouts the entire sermon at one volume gives the people no way to know what matters, because everything is loud and so nothing is. Variety is the whole craft. Drop your voice to a near whisper when the moment is intimate and the room will lean in. Let it rise when the text rises. The most powerful tool you own is contrast, the quiet after the loud, the slow after the fast. A voice that never changes is a voice the mind learns to ignore.

You do not need a trained instrument or a beautiful one. You need a true one, a voice that matches what you are saying, that grieves when the text grieves and lifts when it lifts. Record yourself once and listen. You will hear in five minutes what your people endure every week.

sections.title: Slow Down and Use the Silence
sections.body:
The most common failure in the pulpit is speed. The nervous preacher races, and the people cannot keep up, and the best lines blow past before anyone can feel them.

When a truth is heavy, it needs time to land. You say the hardest sentence in the sermon and then you keep talking, and the sentence never had a chance to do its work because you covered it with the next one. Stop. After the line that matters, give the room silence. A pause that feels agonizing to you, two full seconds, three, is the gift that lets the truth settle into a person. The amateur fears silence and fills every gap. The seasoned preacher knows the pause is not empty. It is where the sermon does its deepest work, in the quiet you had the nerve to leave.

Slow down generally, and then slow down further at the turns. Speed is the sound of a man who does not trust his material. Let the weight of what you are saying set the pace, and let the silence carry what your words cannot.

sections.title: Lift Your Eyes Off the Page
sections.body:
Preaching is not reading aloud. It is one person speaking to other persons, and that cannot happen through the top of your head.

The preacher buried in his manuscript, eyes down, voice aimed at the lectern, has broken the only connection that makes preaching what it is. The people need your eyes. Not a sweep over their heads to the back wall, but real contact, one face and then another, the way you would speak to a single person across a table. When you look a man in the eye and say the thing he needs to hear, it arrives with a weight no glance at the page can carry. This is why knowing your material matters more than any other delivery skill. You cannot connect with eyes that are trapped on paper.

Whether you use full notes or none, you must know the sermon well enough to look up for the lines that matter most. Find the faces. Speak to them. Let them see that you are not reciting at them but pleading with them, because you are.

sections.title: Presence You Cannot Fake
sections.body:
All the technique in the world cannot manufacture the one thing that makes preaching land. The people can tell whether you believe it.

Presence is not charisma. It is not stage skill. It is the visible evidence that the man preaching has been gripped by what he is saying, that this truth has cost him something, that he is not performing a conviction but carrying one. A congregation forgives clumsy gestures and an ordinary voice. It will not follow a man who is plainly untouched by his own message. The preacher who has wept over the text in the study, who has let it indict him before he aimed it at anyone else, walks into the pulpit with an authority no amount of polish provides. They are watching to see if it is real.

So the deepest work on your delivery is not done on Sunday. It is done in the study, alone, when you let the Word do its work on you first. Improve your voice and your pacing and your eyes, all of it. But know that the thing the people are really reading is whether you mean it. There is no technique for that. There is only the cost.
